title: Four routes to one gradient number, and why the one that re-integrates the state backwards can fail
summary: Training a Neural ODE needs the derivative of a loss through an ODE solve. These figures show the forward pass with its solver steps, the adjoint equation integrated backward on the Van der Pol oscillator, four ways of computing the same number, the instability of re-integrating the state in reverse time, and the commuting diagram that explains when discretize-then-optimize and optimize-then-discretize agree.

media.alt: Three panels in a row. Left, titled Van der Pol, mu equals 1, state forward, adjoint backward: two solid curves for the state and two dashed curves for the adjoint over time from 0 to 3. Middle, an orange shaded integrand curve whose title gives the gradient dL over d mu as the integral of a transposed times f_mu dt equal to minus 0.512749. Right, titled four routes to one number: four bars, all the same height near minus 0.51, labelled adjoint with stored state, finite differences, forward sensitivities and adjoint with re-integrated state.

read_the_figure.question: Are the different gradient computations consistent, and what happens to the one that reconstructs the state backward in time?
read_the_figure.axes: Adjoint on Van der Pol: time 0 to 3 against state and adjoint components; the integrand panel gives the contribution a^T f_mu at each time whose area is the gradient. Four routes: bars of dL/dmu with differences below 1e-6. Instability figures: decay rate s of the fast mode (horizontal) against relative gradient error or reconstruction error on log axes with the line 1e-13 e^{sT}. Convergence figures: step size h against relative error for Euler, Heun and RK4.
look_at: Left panel: the state runs forward from time 0 to 3 and the adjoint (dashed) is integrated from time 3 back to 0, starting from the derivative of the loss; they are plotted on the same axis.
Middle panel: the gradient is the area under the integrand, negative in the first half of the interval and positive later; the printed value is -0.512749.
Four routes: adjoint with the stored forward state, finite differences, forward sensitivities and adjoint with the state re-integrated backwards all give -0.51274938 to about 1e-6.

Instability: the gradient error of the adjoint with the stored state stays near 1e-10 as the decay rate s of a fast mode grows to 30 (T = 2), while the error of the adjoint that re-integrates the state climbs like 1e-13 e^{sT} to order one and beyond; the state itself cannot be recovered going backward (reconstruction error follows the same line).
Re-integration still: the true fast and slow components decay forward; integrated backward from the end the reconstructed state leaves the true one at about time 1.6 and stays at zero, clipped.

Two routes diagram: continuous problem, differentiate, continuous gradient, discretize, OTD gradient, and the other way around ending at the DTO gradient, the exact gradient of the discrete loss; the diagram commutes only as h goes to zero, and the mismatch is of order h^p, larger when state reintegration is unstable.

Convergence: DTO's error against the continuous gradient falls as h^p for Euler, Heun and RK4; OTD with a re-integrated state is orders worse and Euler overflows at small step counts; DTO agrees with finite differences of the discrete loss to the 1e-10 floor.

Forward-pass anatomy: log variables with the accepted steps of dopri5 (7) and RK4 (30 steps of 0.1) as tick marks and a step size traced against time for a smooth model and a stiff model; the solver setting is part of the model.
read_the_figure.proves: The gradient can be obtained four ways that agree to six digits on a mild problem. They do not agree on a problem with a fast decaying mode, where reconstructing the state backward amplifies the error exponentially. The exact gradient of what was computed (DTO) is always consistent with finite differences of the discrete loss.
if_wrong: Adjoint with re-integrated state disagreeing with the others: reverse-time instability.
Finite differences with a step far from 1e-6 relative: truncation or round-off noise.
A gradient that changes with the solver tolerance: the solver setting is part of the model.
Mixing OTD and DTO without saying which: the numbers differ at order h^p.
must_check: That the gradient method (stored state, re-integration, discretize-then-optimize) is stated.
That the stiffness of the problem is stated when reconstructing backward.
That tolerances for the forward and backward solves are given separately.
That a finite-difference step is stated.

terms.meaning: The vector a(t) = dL/dy(t) that obeys a linear ODE backward in time.
The derivative of the state with respect to a parameter, integrated forward alongside the state.
Differentiate the discrete numerical scheme exactly (backpropagate through the solver).
Derive the continuous adjoint ODE and then discretize it.
The difference between the true state and the state obtained by integrating backward from the end.

remember: The adjoint obeys da/dt = -a^T df/dy, integrated from T to 0.
dL/dtheta = -integral from 0 to T of a^T df/dtheta dt.
Backward integration of a decaying mode grows like exp(s (T - t)).
DTO is the exact gradient of the discrete loss; OTD differs at order h^p.
The solver setting (tolerance, step size) is part of the model being differentiated.

steps.title: The adjoint equation and the gradient
steps.tex: \frac{\mathrm da}{\mathrm dt}=-a^{\mathsf T}\frac{\partial f}{\partial y},\ a(T)=\frac{\partial L}{\partial y(T)},\qquad \frac{\mathrm dL}{\mathrm d\mu}=-\int_{0}^{T}\!a^{\mathsf T}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mu}\,\mathrm dt
steps.note: The integrand a^T f_mu is the middle panel; its signed area is the printed gradient (up to the sign convention used in the title).

steps.title: Why re-integrating the state backwards is unstable
steps.note: Running time backward turns a decaying mode into a growing one, so a rounding error of 1e-13 at T becomes 1e-13 e^{sT}: for s = 15 and T = 2 that is 1e-13 times 1e13, order one. This is the dotted line of the instability figures (computed).

steps.title: Finite differences and their best step
steps.note: The finite-difference bar agrees with the others to about 1e-6, the typical accuracy of a central difference on a smooth problem.

steps.title: DTO commutes with the discrete problem, OTD only in the limit
steps.note: The diagram's vertical arrow: the OTD gradient and the DTO gradient differ by an amount that shrinks with h, so the two routes agree only as the step goes to zero.

worked.title: Size of the backward reconstruction error
worked.problem: A fast mode has decay rate s = 15 and the horizon is T = 2. Starting from a rounding error of 1e-13 at time T, how large is the reconstruction error at time 0?
worked.answer: About 1: the reconstructed state has an order-one error at the initial time, so the gradient that uses it is meaningless.

analyze.q: Why must the adjoint be integrated backward in time while the state goes forward?
The re-integrated state in the animation clips at +-3 and then stays flat. What does that tell you about the quality of any gradient computed from it?
analyze.hint: It no longer resembles the state.

analyze.q: What does 'the diagram commutes only as h goes to 0' mean for a practitioner choosing between DTO and OTD?
analyze.hint: Which gradient is the gradient of the loss you actually minimize.

evaluate.q: A library offers an adjoint that re-integrates the state to save memory. When is that a bad idea?
Is agreement of four routes at six digits on Van der Pol evidence that the method is safe on stiff problems?

create: Run the four-routes experiment on y' = -s y with s = 1, 10, 30 and plot the error of each against s.
Design a check that detects an unstable re-integration from the forward solve alone.

checks.answer: The derivative of the loss with respect to the final state.
About 4.9e8: errors are amplified by that factor going backward.

checks.q: Why does the stored-state adjoint stay accurate for large s?
checks.answer: It uses the forward solution at each time, which is computed stably (forward decay), so no error growth occurs.

checks.q: DTO is the exact gradient of the discrete loss. Is it also the gradient of the continuous loss?
checks.answer: Only in the limit h to 0; the difference is O(h^p) as the convergence figure shows.

checks.q: Propose a memory-saving scheme that avoids unstable reconstruction.
checks.answer: Store the state at a few checkpoints and recompute segments forward between them when needed.
